overview.description: Hollywood Gin is a popular scoring variation of Gin Rummy. Instead of playing a single game, players record scores for three separate games simultaneously on a single score sheet. This format increases the strategic depth and the excitement of a match by allowing a single win to contribute to multiple game totals.

history.origins: Developed in the 1930s-40s in the United States, particularly among the elite social circles of New York and Hollywood. It became the professional standard for competitive Gin Rummy matches.
timeline: 1940s: Becomes the standard way to play Gin Rummy in card rooms.
1950s: Immortalized in literature and cinema as the 'serious' card game.
Present: The preferred scoring method for organized Gin tournaments.
history.evolution: The base game (Gin Rummy) remained largely the same, but the Hollywood scoring system was invented to mitigate the 'luck of the draw' by extending the match over three games.
history.cultural: Associated with mid-century sophistication and the Golden Age of Hollywood.

setup.players: Two players. Each receives ten cards per hand. The first dealer is chosen by drawing from the shuffled pack (lower card deals); thereafter the winner of the previous hand deals. In serious play both players shuffle and the non-dealer cuts.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Ranking: K-Q-J-10...A (Aces are always low).
setup.dealing: The first dealer is chosen randomly by drawing cards from the shuffled pack - the player who draws the lower card deals.

rules.objective: Win the majority of the three games being played simultaneously.
rules.gameplay: Play follows standard Gin Rummy: each turn a player draws one card from the stock or the top of the discard pile, then discards one card (if drawing from discard, must discard a different card). Players form melds (sets of equal rank or runs in the same suit) and reduce deadwood. A player may knock when deadwood is 10 or less by discarding face down and exposing their hand; the opponent may lay off cards on the knocker's melds unless the knocker went gin. Scoring: knocker scores the difference in deadwood, or the opponent scores the difference plus 10 for an undercut; going gin scores 20 plus the opponent's deadwood. Hollywood scoring: three games are tracked on one score sheet. The first hand won is recorded in Game 1 only; the second win in Games 1 and 2; the third and all subsequent wins in all three games. Each game runs to 100 points then receives game and box bonuses; when all three games are finished the totals are summed for the match score.

Winning condition: Win the majority of the three games being played simultaneously.

strategy.basic: Winning the first hand is extremely valuable as it 'opens' your first column and gets you closer to opening the second and third.
strategy.intermediate: If you have a large lead in Game 1 but are trailing in Games 2 and 3, you may play more conservatively to 'lock in' the first game win while trying to gain ground in the others.
strategy.advanced: Managing the 'knock' timing across multiple game states. If your opponent is close to 100 in Game 1, you might take higher risks to prevent them from taking that specific game bonus.
tips: A 'Slam' (winning every hand in a game) is much harder in Hollywood Gin but results in massive total match scores.
The 'Undercut' bonus is especially impactful when it applies across three columns.

engine.deckDescription: A standard 52-card French deck with four suits and thirteen ranks per suit; no jokers. Hollywood Gin is played with three simultaneous gin rummy games; players aim to win the majority of the three hands.
engine.suitDescription: The four French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades) each contain thirteen cards. Melds are sets of three or more of the same rank or runs of three or more in the same suit.
engine.rankDescription: Standard ranks Ace through King in each suit; Ace may count high or low in runs. Unmatched cards (deadwood) are summed by face value; the goal is to reduce deadwood and knock or go gin.
